draft.title: Hindu environmental ethics
card: Many Hindus believe the divine is present in all things, including rivers, mountains, trees and animals. Nature is therefore seen as sacred and not only as a resource.
the principle of non-harm to living beings. Many Hindus apply it to animals and the wider natural world, which supports care for the environment.
The Ganges is honoured as the goddess Ganga, and many Hindus treat the cow with respect. These practices show how belief shapes the way people treat nature.
Hindus may draw on these beliefs in different ways, so views and actions vary across communities. Many, though not all, link their faith to caring for the environment.
draft.remember: Many Hindus respect nature because the divine is in all things and ahimsa calls for non-harm.

a.q: Which belief most directly leads many Hindus to see a river as sacred?
opts: The divine is present in all things, including nature
The divine is found only in temples and holy books
The divine is separate from the physical world
The divine is present only in living people
a.why: If the divine is present in all things, then a river can be honoured as sacred, as the Ganges is honoured as the goddess Ganga. The belief that the divine is found only in temples is tempting, but the card says the divine is in rivers, mountains, trees and animals too.
a.clue: Think about where the divine is found.

b.q: Priya, a Hindu in Pune, avoids harming insects and animals in her garden and says this is part of caring for the Earth. Which principle is she mainly applying?
opts: Ahimsa, the principle of non-harm to living beings
Moksha, the release from the cycle of rebirth
Varna, the duty set by a person's social class
Puja, worship carried out at a home shrine
b.why: Avoiding harm to animals and insects is an application of ahimsa, which many Hindus extend to the natural world. Puja is a Hindu practice of worship, but it is not the principle of non-harm that Priya is acting on.
b.clue: Which principle is about not harming living beings?

a.best: The divine is present in all things, including nature

b.best: Ahimsa, the principle of non-harm to living beings

problems.detail: The clue 'Which principle is about not harming living beings?' repeats the gloss attached to the right option ('the principle of non-harm to living beings'). A student can match the words without knowing the idea.

Puja belongs to point 5 (a significant Hindu practice), but the option defines it ('worship carried out at a home shrine') and the why explains it again, instead of only mentioning it. The definition is also too narrow, because puja is also performed in temples.
'Varna, the duty set by a person's social class' is inaccurate. Varna is the social class itself; the duty linked to it is varna dharma (svadharma).
